analysis.one_liner: Caps steel imports at pre-crisis levels for three years and requires importers to get licenses.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 289-141 with 204 cosponsors, but the Senate failed a cloture vote 42-57 in June 1999, killing it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the President to cut steel imports to the average monthly level of the 36 months before July 1997, using quotas, tariff surcharges, or negotiated export limits, for three years. Importers would need a license from Commerce, and Customs could turn away steel above the caps. It was aimed at the surge of cheap imported steel in 1998 that idled mills and laid off workers in steel towns.
analysis.who_benefits: Steelworkers and steel communities, particularly integrated steel producers and the United Steelworkers, plus downstream industries that lobby alongside them. Consumers and steel-using industries would pay more.

how_it_helps.text: Caps monthly steel imports at the average tonnage of the 36 months before July 1997, roughly pre-crisis levels, for three years [S2][S3].
Lets Customs refuse entry to steel above allowable levels, aiming to stabilize mills and jobs hit by the 1998 import surge.

analysis.who_pays: Steel-using industries (autos, construction, appliances) and consumers would pay higher prices; trading partners could retaliate.

drawbacks.text: Raises costs for steel-using industries and consumers; trading partners could retaliate. The Ways and Means Committee reported it adversely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Real relief for steelworkers, but concentrated gains at broad costs to steel users and consumers; critics said it violated trade commitments and raised prices.

outcome.mechanism: Passed the House 289-141, but the Senate never voted on the bill itself: a cloture motion on the motion to proceed failed 42-57 on June 22, 1999, blocking consideration.

narrative.text: The Ways and Means Committee reported the bill adversely by voice vote in March 1999, but the House passed it 289-141 under a closed rule [S5][S6].
In the Senate, a cloture vote on the motion to proceed failed 42-57 on June 22, 1999, with 15 Republicans and 27 Democrats in favor, blocking any floor debate or vote [S7].
The bill never received an up-or-down vote in the Senate and died at the end of the 106th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-importing industries and steel consumers won; steelworkers and steel towns lost out on the import relief.

for.name: Rep. Peter Visclosky
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and pushed it through the House.

against.name: 57 Senate opponents of cloture
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture on the motion to proceed, 42-57, keeping the bill off the floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Reported the bill adversely by voice vote.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was bipartisan (197 of 211 Democrats and 91 of 221 Republicans yes), while the Senate cloture failure split both parties: 27 of 45 Democrats and only 15 of 55 Republicans voted for cloture.

industries.note: Import caps would reduce competition and support prices and employment at U.S. mills, though at higher costs to steel users.

industries.industry: Steel-importing and steel-using industries (autos, appliances, construction)
industries.note: Higher steel prices raise input costs, which are passed to consumers.
